alignment.note: The Syriac ܘܐܙܠ fuses the conjunction and the verb 'and he went' into a single prefixed form, which is why index 0 is shared with the preceding conjunction group; Greek ἀπῆλθεν and Latin abiit render the perfective departure equivalently.

Greek μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ and Latin cum illo are two-word prepositional phrases, whereas Syriac ܥܡܗ compactly suffixes the pronoun to the preposition — a synthetic versus analytic rendering of the same comitative sense.

The Peshitta explicitly supplies the proper name ܝܫܘܥ ('Jesus') as the subject of the departure, whereas both the Greek and the Vulgate leave the subject implicit in the verb. This is a typical Syriac clarifying expansion to remove pronominal ambiguity.

Greek ἠκολούθει and Latin sequebatur use a single imperfect verb 'was following'; Syriac employs the periphrastic ܕܒܝܩ ܗܘܐ (passive participle plus the auxiliary ܗܘܐ), a characteristic Syriac construction expressing durative past action.

Greek συνέθλιβον and Latin comprimebant are single imperfect-tense verbs 'were pressing in'; the Syriac again uses a periphrastic ܚܒܨܝܢ ܗܘܘ (active participle plus the plural auxiliary ܗܘܘ) to convey the same durative, plural action of the crowd.
All three attest the accusative/dative object 'him'; the Greek closes the pericope with a paragraph mark (¶), a purely editorial division absent in the Syriac and Latin token streams.
